To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the effect of fiber on ileal and total tract AA digestibility in pigs is rather small and that the bacterial AA contribution to the feces is not a major factor influencing ileal and total-tract digestibility of AA in pigs.
cellulose, starch, and pectin supplementation had no significant effect (p>0.05) on the standardized ileal digestibilities of crude protein and amino acids in growing pigs.
the inclusion of cellulose, but not starch and pectine, in a diet for pigs results in higher bacterial contribution to fecal AA.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of cellulose, cellulose, starch on standardized ilea digestibility and apparent total tract amino acid digestibilities and bacterial contribution of amino acids in feces of growing pigs.
the effect of different dietary fiber sources on the bacterial AA composition of MBM and the bacterial contribution to fecal AA in growing pigs.
the development of a new, non-invasive method to measure the digestibility of nutrients in the gastrointestinal tract of pigs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects of dietary fiber on SID and ATTD are small and that endogenous AA losses are not affected by dietary fiber.
cellulose and pectorin have a negative effect on AA digestibility in the large intestine, whereas starch has a positive effect.
the effects of celluloses, starches and pectins on SID are rather small, and the effects on ATTD and bacterial AA composition in feces are not consistent and depend on the type of AA.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effects of dietary fiber on AA availability are rather small and the bacterial contribution of AA to total fecal output is not affected by the type of dietary fiber.
cellulose, starch, and pectin have different effects on the bacterial activity in the large intestines, which is reflected in the bacterial AA composition of feces.

cellulose and pectorins can be used as fiber sources in pig diets, as they did not reduce AA digestibility, but that starch should be limited to a certain amount to prevent a decrease in AA digestibility.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the effects of dietary fiber on AA digestibility are rather small, and that the effects of the dietary fiber source on AA digestibility in pigs are small compared with the effects of the source of the dietary fiber on the bacterial AA composition and bacterial contribution of AA in the large gut.
cellulose, starch, and pectin have only small effects on SID of AA, but can affect the AA content and AA profile of MBM in the large intestine.

the effects of celluloses, starch and pectorins on the ATTD of amino acids in the large intestine are not consistent, which may explain the inconsistent effects of these dietary fibers on growth performance of pigs.
